claim: Pew measured a roughly 15-fold gap between mean and median video performance among popular YouTube channels: the average video received 58,358 views in its first week while 50% of videos received fewer than 3,860.
stance_target: Mean-based creator statistics are systematically misleading and the median creator outcome is an order of magnitude below the average
scope_conditions: Unit is videos, not creators, and only from channels with 250,000+ subscribers, i.e. the top tier of the platform; the median across all channels would be far lower still
quoted_support: each individual video received an average of 58,358 views in its first week, although 50% received fewer than 3,860 views

claim: Within the 56% of popular channels that were active, output was itself highly concentrated: 31% posted exactly one video, 55% posted between two and nine, and the 14% that posted ten or more published 75% of all videos.
stance_target: Sustained high-volume production is confined to a small minority even among established creators
scope_conditions: Among the 24,632 active channels in a single week, January 2019; 250,000+ subscriber frame
quoted_support: Just 14% posted 10 or more videos during the study period, but this subset of channels was responsible for publishing 75% of all of the videos uploaded by popular channels during the week.

claim: Pew found English-language videos from popular channels earned a median of 13,316 first-week views versus 3,028 for videos in other languages, a 4.4-fold median advantage, even though non-English videos made up over 80% of all output.
stance_target: That findings about creator economics measured on Anglophone content generalize to non-English-language markets such as Southeast Asia
scope_conditions: Same platform, same week, same channel-size frame, so the comparison is unusually clean; Pew does not decompose the non-English group by country or language, so the gap cannot be attributed to any specific market; measures views, not revenue, and regional CPM differences would widen the earnings gap further
quoted_support: English-language videos comprised just 17% of the videos that were published by popular channels during the week, but they received 28% of all of the views received by popular-channel videos during their first week after being published.
numbers: English 17% of videos but 28% of views
region: Global; English versus all other languages

claim: A majority of Pew's active popular channels were not Anglophone: 67% posted exclusively in languages other than English, 28% exclusively in English and 5% in both, so the most-cited Western YouTube census is drawn from a predominantly non-English channel population.
stance_target: The assumption that Pew's YouTube research is US or Western-only evidence
scope_conditions: Language composition is published; country composition is not, so this establishes linguistic breadth without establishing regional representation and no Southeast Asian country share is reported anywhere; separately, Pew's top-500 video comparison was restricted to videos viewable in the United States, the API default, which is a genuine US-centric artefact
quoted_support: And within this subset of active channels, 28% posted videos exclusively in English. Meanwhile, 67% posted videos exclusively in languages other than English, and 5% posted videos in multiple languages including English.
numbers: 17% of all videos fully in English
top-500 list restricted to US-viewable videos
